etymology: Anglo-Saxon neahra, comparative of neah, near — closer in place, time, or relation.
biblical_def:
And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I. And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.

Boaz's nearer names a legal and moral obstacle before it can become a love story: the whole plan of redemption in Ruth must wait on a kinsman nearer than Boaz relinquishing his right first. The word governs the entire chapter's suspense, and its resolution at the city gate is the hinge on which the rest of the book turns. Paul's nearer is a different clock entirely — not a rival claim to settle but a certainty to spur obedience: our salvation is nearer than when we believed, and the shrinking distance is itself the argument for waking out of sleep. Both uses treat nearer as something to act on, not merely notice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from NEAR: not far distant in place, time, or degree of relation; comparative degree, closer.
webster_full: NEAR, a. Not far distant in place; close at hand.
Closely related by blood; as, a near kinsman.
Close in time; approaching.
NEARER, a. Comparative of Near; closer in place, time, or kinship.
Applied in Scripture both to legal kinship (Ruth) and to the approach of the last things (Romans).
scriptures: Rut 3:12
And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I.
And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.
corruption_summary: A sense of urgency has largely drained out of both applications: kinship obligation is treated as sentiment rather than a nearer claim to be honored in order, and the nearness of salvation is treated as a doctrine to affirm rather than a reason to wake.
corruption_paragraphs: Boaz will not proceed until the nearer kinsman's claim is properly settled, a picture of ordered obligation modern individualism finds slow and needless. The text disagrees; the nearer claim is honored precisely because it is real, not brushed aside for convenience.

Romans 13:11 turns nearer into an alarm clock, not a comfort. Every generation that hears our salvation nearer than when we believed as merely reassuring, rather than urgent, has missed the verb attached to it: awake.
roots_summary: From ga'al (Heb.), to redeem, tied to kinship nearness in Ruth, and engys (Gk.), near, used by Paul of the approaching day.
roots_lines: Nearer in Ruth is a legal claim that must be settled in order.
The nearer kinsman's right is honored, not bypassed, by Boaz.
Nearer in Romans measures time, not kinship.
Salvation nearer than when we believed is offered as a reason to wake, not merely to rest assured.
Both uses treat nearer as a call to right action, not a passive fact.
usage: A kinsman nearer than I — the obstacle that must be resolved before redemption proceeds.
Our salvation nearer than when we believed — the ground of Paul's call to wake.
High time to awake out of sleep — the verb nearer is meant to produce.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon hlud, loud — of greater volume or intensity of sound; comparative degree.
biblical_def:
And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice.

Louder and louder, doubled for emphasis, marks Sinai as an event that grew in intensity the longer it continued, not a single clap that quickly faded. The trumpet was not a human instrument sounded by human breath; it waxed, on its own, as the mountain quaked and the LORD descended upon it in fire. Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice in the very next clause of the same verse — the loudness did not drown out dialogue but framed it, terrifying the camp below while remaining, for Moses, the setting of actual conversation. Louder and louder is Sinai's own commentary on itself: this was not a metaphorical thunder but an increasing, deliberate, unbearable volume, calibrated to a holiness no ordinary sound could represent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LOUD: making a great noise; noisy; striking the ear with great force; comparative degree.
webster_full: LOUD, a. Making a great noise; noisy; striking the organs of hearing with great force.
Clamorous; boisterous.
LOUDER, a. Comparative of Loud; of greater volume or force of sound.
Applied in Exodus to the trumpet sound at Sinai, increasing rather than static.
The doubling louder and louder in the Authorized Version denotes continuous, mounting intensity.
scriptures: And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Louder survives as a plain descriptive word tied to one unrepeatable theophany.

The principle to recover is the mismatch modern worship culture sometimes creates: volume borrowed for atmosphere, without the holiness Sinai's louder and louder was actually calibrated to represent. Sinai's loudness terrified precisely because of what it revealed, not merely because it was loud.
roots_summary: From chazaq (Heb.), to grow strong or intense, used of the trumpet's sound waxing rather than merely sounding.
roots_lines: Louder and louder is doubled in the Authorized Version to mark continuous increase.
The trumpet's sound was not of human origin or breath.
Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice, in the same verse as the mounting sound.
The loudness framed real dialogue rather than replacing it.
Sinai's volume was calibrated to holiness, not to spectacle for its own sake.
usage: Waxed louder and louder — continuous, mounting intensity, not a static noise.
Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice — dialogue framed by, not drowned by, the sound.
The doubling in the text is itself part of the description.

pos: v. (past tense of shrink; contracted, drew back or in)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon scrincan, to shrink — to contract, draw back, or diminish, as from injury or fear.
biblical_def:
Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day: because he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh in the sinew that shrank.

The sinew that shrank is Jacob's permanent memorial of the night he wrestled with God and prevailed, yet came away limping — a wound given at the very moment of blessing. Israel's ongoing abstinence from that sinew, unto this day, turns a single ancient injury into a standing national reminder: the man who became Israel was first crippled by the God he wrestled. Shrank names the physical mark left by an encounter no metaphor could fully carry — real contact, real cost, and a blessing that did not undo the limp but was received alongside it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SHRINK: to contract, draw back, or become smaller, especially from pain, fear, or injury.
webster_full: SHRINK, v.i. To contract; to draw back or together; to become smaller in bulk.
To withdraw, as from danger or suffering; to recoil.
SHRANK, pret. Contracted; drew back or together; diminished.
Applied in Genesis to the sinew of Jacob's thigh, injured in his wrestling with the angel.
The memorial abstinence from this sinew is noted as continuing to the writer's own day.
scriptures: Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day: because he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh in the sinew that shrank.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Shrank survives as a plain narrative word tied to one deliberately preserved national memorial.

The principle to recover is the pattern the sinew that shrank sets for every real encounter with God: blessing and cost are not always separable, and a limp carried afterward is not evidence the wrestling failed, but evidence that it was real.
roots_summary: From naveh or gid ha-nasheh (Heb.), the sinew of the thigh vein, named uniquely in this verse and nowhere else in the Torah.
roots_lines: Shrank names a physical, lasting injury, not a figure of speech.
The injury came at the moment of Jacob's greatest blessing, not apart from it.
Israel's abstinence from this sinew memorializes the event nationally.
Unto this day marks the custom as still observed when the text was written.
The limp and the new name, Israel, are given in the same encounter.
usage: The sinew which shrank — a permanent physical memorial of Jacob's wrestling.
Unto this day — a custom that outlived the event by generations.
He touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh — the cost given alongside the blessing.

pos: v. (past tense of sink; descended, was submerged)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon sincan, to sink — to descend, especially into water, under weight or judgment.
biblical_def:
The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone.

Moses's song does not soften Pharaoh's army's end. They sank into the bottom as a stone is chosen for its plainness and its totality — a stone does not float, struggle, or resurface, and neither did Egypt's chariots and horsemen. The depths have covered them completes the picture: no rescue, no partial escape, the same sea that had been a wall of deliverance for Israel became, in the same hour, a grave for their pursuers. Sank is the exact word for judgment that is total and final, and Moses sings it, rather than merely narrating it, because the same event that sank Egypt is the event that saved Israel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SINK: to descend below the surface, as in water; to fall or drop, especially by weight; to be overwhelmed.
webster_full: SINK, v.i. To descend below the surface of a fluid; to fall to the bottom.
To fall gradually, as from weakness or exhaustion.
To be overwhelmed; to fail, or suffer ruin.
SANK, pret. Descended below the surface; was submerged; was overwhelmed.
Applied in Exodus 15 to the total destruction of Pharaoh's pursuing army in the sea.
scriptures: Exo 15:5
The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Sank survives as a plain narrative word tied to the exodus's decisive act of judgment.

The principle to recover is the one Moses sings rather than merely states: the same sea, the same hour, was both salvation and judgment, depending entirely on which side of it a man stood. Deliverance and destruction are not always separated by different events.
roots_summary: From tsalal (Heb.), to sink or settle, chosen deliberately alongside the simile as a stone for its total finality.
roots_lines: Sank describes total, final destruction, not a partial setback.
As a stone rules out struggle, floating, or eventual escape.
The depths have covered them completes the totality of the judgment.
The same sea and hour that judged Egypt delivered Israel.
Moses sings this event; he does not merely record it.
usage: They sank into the bottom as a stone — total, final judgment, chosen for its plainness.
The depths have covered them — no partial escape implied.
Sung, not merely narrated, in Moses's own song of deliverance.

pos: part. (present participle of use; employing, making use of)
etymology: Latin uti, to use — the act of employing a thing for its purpose, whether rightly or wrongly.
biblical_def:
Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men? As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.

Paul's two uses of using sit on opposite sides of an argument. Colossians dismisses man-made rules about handling created things — touch not, taste not, handle not — by noting flatly that these things perish with the using, so no religious weight can rightly hang on how they are used. Peter's using belongs to a different danger entirely: liberty itself, rightly possessed, can be turned into a cloke of maliciousness, using freedom to disguise sin as freedom. Between the two stands the whole Christian doctrine of things indifferent — perishable objects carry no holiness in their handling, and real liberty carries real responsibility in its using.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from USE: to employ for some purpose; to make use of; to practice habitually; participial form denoting the act in progress.
webster_full: USE, v.t. To employ for the attainment of some purpose; to make use of.
To practice customarily; to accustom.
USING, ppr. Employing; making use of; practicing.
Applied by Paul to perishable things (Colossians) and by Peter to Christian liberty.
Neither text condemns using itself; both condemn a particular misuse of it.
scriptures: Col 2:22
Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men?
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
corruption_summary: Modern legalism and modern license repeat, in reverse, the two errors Paul and Peter each addressed: man-made rules about perishable things treated as holy, and Christian liberty invoked to cover for sin it was never meant to disguise.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians answers a legalism that attaches sanctity to the handling of things that perish with the using — food laws, dress codes, and rituals invented by men rather than commanded by God, still current in various forms.

1 Peter answers the opposite error, common wherever grace is preached without corresponding responsibility: freedom's using turned into a cloke of maliciousness, liberty cited as an excuse for exactly the sin it was purchased to end.
roots_summary: From chresis (Gk.), use, in Colossians, and eleutheria, liberty, in 1 Peter — using is the verb applied to both a thing and a freedom.
roots_lines: Using in Colossians dismisses false holiness attached to perishable things.
Using in 1 Peter warns against liberty turned into cover for sin.
Neither passage condemns using as such, only its misuse.
A cloke of maliciousness names the specific danger liberty invites.
Perish with the using is Paul's own argument against elevating created things.
usage: Perish with the using — Paul's dismissal of manufactured holiness in handling things.
Not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness — Peter's warning against abused freedom.
As free... as the servants of God — liberty and service held together, not opposed.

pos: adv. (with violent haste or rage; unrestrained in speed or anger)
etymology: Latin furia, fury, rage — acting with violent, unrestrained force or passion.
biblical_def:
And the watchman told, saying, He came even unto them, and cometh not again: and the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously.

Furiously belongs, in the Authorized Version's most famous use, to a single man's driving so distinctive that a watchman could identify him from a distance by manner alone: the driving is like the driving of Jehu... for he driveth furiously. It is a compliment to nothing but recognizability. Jehu's furious driving matched a furious mission — the violent end of Ahab's dynasty, executed with a zeal that Scripture records without fully commending, since Jehu's later unfaithfulness shows that furious zeal for a right cause is no substitute for a whole heart toward God. Ezekiel's furiously names something darker still, deliberate divine judgment carried out with unrestrained severity against covenant treachery. Furiously, in both, describes intensity without necessarily describing virtue.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FURIOUS: raging; violent; transported with passion or anger; acting with unrestrained force or speed.
webster_full: FURIOUS, a. Raging; violent; transported with passion.
Rushing with impetuous force or speed.
FURIOUSLY, adv. With rage or unrestrained violence; with impetuous haste.
Applied in 2 Kings to Jehu's distinctive, recognizable manner of driving.
Applied in Ezekiel to the unrestrained severity of divine judgment against treachery.
scriptures: And the watchman told, saying, He came even unto them, and cometh not again: and the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously.

And I will set my jealousy against thee, and they shall deal furiously with thee: they shall take away thy nose and thine ears; and thy remnant shall fall by the sword: they shall take thy sons and thy daughters; and thy residue shall be devoured by the fire.
corruption_summary: A culture that prizes intensity and hustle as virtues in themselves risks admiring Jehu's furiously purely for its energy, missing Scripture's own later verdict that his zeal, however effective, did not proceed from a whole heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Jehu's furious driving is memorable precisely because Scripture will not let the reader stop at admiration; the books of Kings go on to record that Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD with all his heart, a warning against mistaking furious energy for faithfulness.

Ezekiel's furiously belongs to a different register entirely, describing judgment, not driving — a reminder that intensity, whatever its source, is not automatically praiseworthy simply for being intense.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew headword; the field is shig'a'on, madness or fury, applied uniquely to Jehu's manner of driving, unmatched elsewhere in Scripture.
roots_lines: Furiously identifies Jehu from a distance, by manner alone.
The word describes intensity, not automatically virtue.
Jehu's zeal executed real judgment yet was later found incomplete.
Ezekiel applies the same word to divine judgment's severity.
Neither use offers furiously as something simply to imitate.
usage: He driveth furiously — intensity distinctive enough to identify a man by it alone.
The driving is like the driving of Jehu — a manner memorable enough to become proverbial.
They shall deal furiously with thee — Ezekiel's application of the same word to judgment.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon thiccra, comparative of thicc, thick — of greater bulk or density.
biblical_def:
And the young men that were grown up with him spake unto him, saying, Thus shalt thou speak unto this people... My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins.

Thicker is the single most quotable line of folly in the whole account of Rehoboam's ruin, and it belongs entirely to the young men's counsel, not merely to the king. Solomon's yoke had been heavy; the people asked for relief; and the answer chosen, over the elders' wiser counsel, was a boast that the new king's little finger would be thicker than his father's loins — his smallest gesture of severity greater than his father's whole strength. The kingdom split the same day. Thicker names arrogance so total it mistakes cruelty for strength, and the text records it without comment, because the outcome supplies all the commentary needed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from THICK: having extent from one surface to its opposite, considerable in that dimension; comparative degree.
webster_full: THICK, a. Having great extent between opposite surfaces; not thin.
Dense; compact; not fluid or diffuse.
THICKER, a. Comparative of Thick; of greater bulk, density, or extent.
Used figuratively in 1 Kings of severity or strength, in a boast comparing father and son.
The comparison is chosen by young counselors to signal harsher rule than the prior reign.
scriptures: And the young men that were grown up with him spake unto him, saying, Thus shalt thou speak unto this people that spake unto thee, saying, Thy father made our yoke heavy, but make thou it lighter unto us; thus shalt thou say unto them, My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Thicker survives as a plain narrative word tied to one of the Old Testament's clearest object lessons in the folly of harsh leadership.

The principle to recover is unusually direct: counsel that recommends cruelty as strength, chosen over wiser and gentler counsel, splits what it was meant to secure. The kingdom of Israel divided the same day this boast was spoken.
roots_summary: No Hebrew headword of doctrinal weight; the significance lies entirely in the boast's content and its immediate, recorded consequence.
roots_lines: Thicker belongs to the young men's counsel, chosen over the elders'.
The boast answers a request for relief from a heavy yoke with a threat of worse.
The kingdom split into two the same day the boast was spoken.
Scripture records the folly without commentary, letting the outcome judge it.
The verse remains a standing warning against mistaking severity for strength.
usage: My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins — folly mistaking cruelty for strength.
Make thou it lighter unto us — the request the boast directly refused.
The kingdom's split the same day is the text's own verdict on the counsel.

pos: adv. (with grave formality; earnestly and with binding weight)
etymology: Latin solemnis, customary, sacred — done with the gravity and binding weight proper to a sacred or formal act.
biblical_def:
And Judah spake unto him, saying, The man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.

Solemnly marks Joseph's warning to his brothers as something more binding than an offhand remark — a protest made with the full gravity of a sworn condition, repeated by Judah to Jacob precisely because its weight cannot be waved away by a father's reluctance. The whole tense standoff over sending Benjamin to Egypt turns on how seriously that solemn protest is taken; Judah's report treats it as settled fact, not negotiable preference. Solemnly, wherever it appears, marks the difference between words that can be revised later and words a hearer is meant to receive as final.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SOLEMN: attended with religious ceremony, or with an appeal to God; marked by seriousness and gravity; earnestly binding.
webster_full: SOLEMN, a. Attended with religious rites, or with an appeal to God; sacred; marked by gravity.
Grave; serious; earnest, as a solemn promise or protest.
SOLEMNLY, adv. With gravity and earnestness; in a manner marked by seriousness and binding weight.
Used in Genesis of Joseph's warning to his brothers concerning Benjamin.
Distinguished from casual speech by the weight it places on the hearer to honor the condition stated.
scriptures: Gen 43:3
And Judah spake unto him, saying, The man did solemnly protest unto us, saying, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Solemnly survives as a plain word for grave, binding speech, and the age has not repurposed it.

The principle worth recovering is the seriousness the word assumes: a generation quick to hedge every promise with escape clauses could stand to recover the category of a protest so solemn it settles the matter, as Joseph's did for Jacob's sons.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew headword; the force is carried by the doubled Hebrew construction the KJV renders solemnly protest, an emphatic, binding warning.
roots_lines: Solemnly marks speech meant to be received as final, not merely earnest.
Joseph's protest is reported by Judah as settled fact.
The condition attached, except your brother be with you, is treated as non-negotiable.
The whole standoff over Benjamin turns on how seriously the protest is taken.
Solemn speech, in Scripture, obligates the hearer, not merely the speaker.
usage: The man did solemnly protest unto us — a binding warning, not a casual remark.
Ye shall not see my face, except your brother be with you — the specific condition made solemn.
Judah reports it as settled, not as something still open to negotiation.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon niwlice, from niwe, new — done a short time ago; freshly.
biblical_def:
So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.

Newly set the watch is the precise, timed detail that makes Gideon's raid a study in exact obedience rather than lucky improvisation. The three hundred did not attack at a convenient hour; they came at the beginning of the middle watch, the exact moment a fresh guard had newly taken its post and the previous one had not yet fully withdrawn, the point of greatest confusion for an army roused from sleep. Three hundred men, trumpets, pitchers, and torches accomplished what an army of thirty-two thousand had already been reduced from, precisely because God had insisted on timing and numbers small enough that no one could credit the victory to human strength.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from NEW: recently made, done, or begun; not of ancient date; adverbial form denoting a very recent action.
webster_full: NEW, a. Recently made, invented, or produced; not existing before.
Fresh; not before used or known.
NEWLY, adv. Recently; freshly; not long since.
Used in Judges of the precise moment a guard had just been posted.
The timing named by newly is part of the narrative's demonstration of exact, deliberate strategy.
scriptures: Jdg 7:19

So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Newly survives as a plain narrative detail of timing in one of Judges' clearest accounts of God's strength made perfect in small numbers.

The principle to recover is the deliberate smallness the timing serves: three hundred men, an exact hour, ordinary pitchers and trumpets, arranged so that no one present could mistake the victory for their own strength.
roots_summary: No Hebrew headword of doctrinal weight; the significance lies in the precise timing the word marks within the narrative of Gideon's three hundred.
roots_lines: Newly marks an exact, deliberate moment, not a vague recency.
The middle watch's fresh guard was the point of greatest confusion.
Three hundred men accomplished what a much larger army had been reduced from.
Trumpets and pitchers, not weapons, were the instruments of the raid.
The smallness of the force was itself the point, not an obstacle overcome.
usage: They had but newly set the watch — the exact, deliberate moment chosen for the raid.
The beginning of the middle watch — timing calculated for maximum confusion.
Trumpets... pitchers — ordinary objects turned into instruments of an extraordinary victory.

pos: adv. (widely, extensively; common to a whole people or place)
etymology: Latin generalis, pertaining to a whole kind or class — spread throughout, not confined to a part.
biblical_def:
There shall be lamentation generally upon all the housetops of Moab, and in the streets thereof: for I have broken Moab like a vessel wherein is no pleasure, saith the LORD.

Generally, in Isaiah's judgment oracle against Moab, describes grief with no exception left standing: lamentation generally upon all the housetops... and in the streets thereof covers every dwelling and every public space, private roof and open road alike. The vessel wherein is no pleasure explains why the grief is so total — Moab has been broken as completely and irreparably as a shattered pot that even its owner would not trouble to mend. Generally, here, is not exaggeration but precision: the judgment named touches the whole of the nation, not merely a part of it, and the lamentation that follows is described as equally comprehensive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from GENERAL: common; widely spread; extending to a whole class or people, not confined to particular instances.
webster_full: GENERAL, a. Common; relating to a whole class or kind; not partial or special.
Widely spread; prevalent; extending to most persons or places.
GENERALLY, adv. In a general manner; extensively; commonly; without exception through a whole class.
Applied in Jeremiah to lamentation covering every housetop and street of a judged nation.
Denotes totality of extent, not merely frequency.
scriptures: There shall be lamentation generally upon all the housetops of Moab, and in the streets thereof: for I have broken Moab like a vessel wherein is no pleasure, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Generally survives as a plain word for total extent, tied to one nation's recorded judgment.

The principle to recover is the totality the prophets were willing to name plainly: a broken vessel wherein is no pleasure describes judgment complete enough that repair is not even contemplated, a sobering counterweight to any theology that expects every judgment to be partial or temporary.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew headword; the force is carried by the phrase kol gagoth, all the roofs, paired with the broken-vessel image of total ruin.
roots_lines: Generally in Jeremiah marks totality of extent, not mere frequency.
All the housetops... and in the streets covers private and public space alike.
The broken vessel image explains the totality of the lamentation.
Wherein is no pleasure signals judgment complete enough not to be repaired.
The word functions as precision, not rhetorical exaggeration.
usage: Lamentation generally upon all the housetops — grief with no exception left standing.
Broken... like a vessel wherein is no pleasure — the reason the lamentation is total.
A judgment named as covering the whole of a nation, not a part of it.
